questions.prompt: List the primitive types in JavaScript.
key_points: There are 7 primitive types

questions.correct_answer: JavaScript has 7 primitive types: string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null and symbol. Primitives are simple values with no methods of their own. Everything that is not a primitive is an object, and that includes arrays, functions and dates.

questions.prompt: How is a primitive different from an object?
key_points: Primitives are copied by value; objects are copied by reference
Primitives cannot be changed; objects can be changed
Two objects are equal only when they are the same object
Primitives have no properties of their own; their methods work through temporary wrapper objects
questions.correct_answer: A primitive is a single value that is copied when you assign it, so changing the copy never touches the original. An object is copied by reference, so two variables can point to the same object and see each other's changes. Primitives cannot be changed: string methods return new strings. Two objects are only equal with === when they are the same object, even if their contents match.

questions.prompt: Why does changing an object's property inside a function change it outside, but reassigning the parameter does not?
key_points: The function receives a copy of the reference, not a copy of the object
Changing a property changes the shared object, so the caller sees it
Reassigning the parameter only points the local variable at a new value
A primitive argument can never be changed through the parameter
questions.correct_answer: JavaScript passes a copy of the value, and for an object that value is a reference. So the parameter and the caller's variable point to the same object, and setting a property changes that one shared object. Reassigning the parameter only changes where the local variable points; the caller's variable still points to the old object. A primitive argument is copied, so nothing inside the function can change the caller's value. This is why React state should be copied, not mutated.

questions.prompt: Which line throws an error?

What are the differences between `var`, `let` and `const`?
key_points: `var` is function scoped; `let` and `const` are block scoped
`const` cannot be reassigned; `let` and `var` can
`var` can be declared twice in the same scope; `let` and `const` cannot
`var` is hoisted and set to undefined; `let` and `const` are in the temporal dead zone until their line
questions.correct_answer: var is scoped to the whole function, while let and const are scoped to the nearest block. let and var can be reassigned, but const cannot. var can be declared twice in one scope without an error; let and const throw. All three are hoisted, but var starts as undefined, while let and const cannot be used before their line (the temporal dead zone).

questions.prompt: Can you change a `const` object? Explain.
key_points: Yes, its properties can be changed
`const` only stops the variable from being reassigned
The variable holds a reference; the object itself is not protected

questions.correct_answer: Yes. const means the variable cannot be pointed at a different value, but the object it points to can still be changed. So user.name = 'Bob' or arr.push(3) works on a const. To stop changes to the object you use Object.freeze, which only freezes the top level, not nested objects.

questions.prompt: Why do modern codebases use `const` by default, `let` when needed, and avoid `var`?
key_points: `const` tells the reader the variable is never reassigned, so code is easier to follow
`let` is used only when a value really changes, such as a loop counter
`var` leaks out of blocks because it is function scoped, which causes bugs such as with loops and callbacks
`var` allows silent redeclaration and becomes a `window` property at the top level
questions.correct_answer: const makes it clear that a variable is never reassigned, so the reader has less to track, and accidental reassignment throws. let is kept for values that really change, like counters. var is avoided because it is function scoped, so it leaks out of if blocks and loops; a var loop with setTimeout prints the same number every time. var can also be redeclared silently and adds properties to window at the top level.

questions.prompt:
console.log(typeof greet);
function greet() {}
What is hoisting?
key_points: Declarations are set up before the code in a scope runs
`var` is hoisted and starts as undefined
Function declarations are hoisted with their whole body, so they can be called early
Code is not really moved; it is how the engine prepares the scope
questions.correct_answer: Hoisting means the engine sets up all declarations in a scope before it runs that scope's code. A var exists from the start of its function with the value undefined. A function declaration is hoisted with its body, so you can call it before its line. The code is not physically moved; this is just how scopes are prepared.

questions.prompt: Why does using a `let` variable before its line throw an error?
key_points: `let` and `const` are hoisted but not initialized
From the start of the block to the declaration line is the temporal dead zone
Reading the variable in the temporal dead zone throws a ReferenceError (cannot access before initialization)
This catches bugs that `var` would hide by giving undefined
questions.correct_answer: let and const are hoisted, so the engine knows about them from the start of the block, but they are not given a value until their line runs. The time before that line is called the temporal dead zone. Any read or write in that zone throws a ReferenceError saying you cannot access the variable before initialization. This is on purpose: var would silently give undefined and hide the bug.

questions.prompt: Compare calling these before their lines: a function declaration, a function expression stored in a `var`, and a function expression stored in a `const`.
key_points: The function declaration works, because the whole function is hoisted
The `var` expression throws a TypeError, because the variable is undefined at that point
The `const` expression throws a ReferenceError, because the variable is in the temporal dead zone
For expressions only the variable name is hoisted, never the function
questions.correct_answer: A function declaration is hoisted with its body, so calling it early works. With var sayHi = function () {}, only the variable is hoisted and it is undefined, so calling it throws a TypeError: sayHi is not a function. With const, the variable is in the temporal dead zone, so calling it throws a ReferenceError. In both expression cases the function value only exists once its line has run.

questions.prompt: What is variable shadowing?
options: An inner scope declares a variable with the same name as an outer one, hiding the outer one inside that scope
A variable that is declared but never used

questions.correct_answer: An inner scope declares a variable with the same name as an outer one, hiding the outer one inside that scope

questions.prompt: What are global, function and block scope?
key_points: Global scope: declared outside every function and block, visible everywhere
Function scope: declared inside a function, visible only in that function; `var` is function scoped
Block scope: `let` and `const` inside `{ }` are visible only in that block
questions.correct_answer: Scope decides where a variable can be used. Global scope is the outermost one: variables declared there can be read everywhere. Function scope means a variable declared inside a function is only visible in that function, and var always works this way. Block scope means let and const declared inside braces, such as an if or a loop, are only visible inside those braces.

questions.prompt: What is the scope chain? Give an example.
key_points: Each scope is linked to the scope it was written in
Lookup starts in the current scope and moves outward up to global
The first match wins, so inner variables hide (shadow) outer ones
If no scope has the variable, a ReferenceError is thrown
questions.correct_answer: Every scope is linked to the outer scope it was written inside, and these links form the scope chain. When code reads a variable, JavaScript looks in the current scope first, then the outer one, and so on up to global. The first match is used, so an inner variable with the same name hides the outer one. For example, an inner function can read a variable from its outer function and from global scope. If nothing matches, it throws a ReferenceError.

questions.prompt: What is lexical scope, and how does it explain stale values inside `useEffect` callbacks or event handlers in React?
key_points: Scope is decided by where code is written, not where it is called
A function keeps access to the variables of the scope it was created in
A callback created during one render sees that render's state values
Fix with the right dependency array, a functional state update, or a ref
questions.correct_answer: Lexical scope means a function's variables are decided by where the function is written, not where it is called. A function keeps access to the variables around it when it was created. In React every render creates new handler and effect functions that see that render's state. If an effect with an empty dependency array starts an interval, its callback keeps the first render's state forever. You fix it by listing dependencies, using a functional update like setCount(c => c + 1), or reading from a ref.

What is the difference between `==` and `===`? Which one should you use?
key_points: `===` checks value and type, with no conversion
`==` converts the values to a common type before comparing
`==` gives surprising results, such as `0 == ""` being true
Use `===` by default; `x == null` is a common exception to check null or undefined
questions.correct_answer: === is strict equality: it is true only when both value and type are the same. == is loose equality: it first converts the values to a common type, so 0 == '' and '1' == 1 are true. Those conversions cause bugs, so use === by default. A common exception is value == null, which checks for both null and undefined at once.

questions.prompt: Why is `"5" + 1` equal to `"51"`, but `"5" - 1` equal to `4`?
key_points: `+` with a string joins strings, so 1 becomes "1"
`-` only works on numbers, so "5" becomes 5
Other math operators like `*`, `/` and `%` also convert to numbers
This automatic conversion is called implicit type coercion
questions.correct_answer: The + operator does two jobs: adding numbers and joining strings. If either side is a string, it joins them, so 1 is turned into '1' and the result is '51'. The - operator only does maths, so JavaScript turns '5' into the number 5 and gives 4. *, / and % behave the same way as -. This automatic conversion is called implicit type coercion.

questions.prompt: Form inputs give you strings. How do you compare or add their values safely, and what goes wrong if you do not?
key_points: Convert explicitly with `Number()`, `parseInt` or `parseFloat` (or `valueAsNumber`)
Adding two strings joins them: "2" + "3" is "23"
Comparing two strings with `<` compares them character by character, so "10" < "9" is true
Check for NaN with `Number.isNaN` after converting
Use `===` after converting so both types match
questions.correct_answer: Input values are always strings, so convert them first with Number(), parseInt or parseFloat, or read valueAsNumber on number inputs. Without that, '2' + '3' gives '23', and '10' < '9' is true because strings are compared character by character. After converting, check the result with Number.isNaN, because empty or invalid text becomes NaN. Then compare with === so both sides are numbers.

questions.prompt: What do `&&` and `||` return? Explain with examples.
key_points: They return one of their operands, not always a boolean
`||` returns the first truthy value, or the last value if none is truthy
`&&` returns the first falsy value, or the last value if all are truthy
Used for defaults like `name || "guest"` and for conditional rendering
questions.correct_answer: && and || return one of the values you give them, not necessarily true or false. || returns the first truthy value, or the last value if all are falsy, so name || 'guest' gives a default. && returns the first falsy value, or the last value if all are truthy, so isLoggedIn && user.name gives the name only when logged in. React uses && for conditional rendering for the same reason.

questions.prompt: Why can `{count && <p/>}` render a `0` in React, and how do you fix it? When is `??` better than `||`?
key_points: `&&` returns `0` itself when count is 0
React renders numbers, but renders nothing for false, null and undefined
Fix with `count > 0 &&`, `Boolean(count) &&`, or a ternary
`??` only falls back for null or undefined, so 0 and "" are kept
`||` replaces every falsy value, which is wrong when 0 or "" is a valid value
questions.correct_answer: When count is 0, count && <p/> returns 0, and React renders numbers, so a 0 appears. React renders nothing for false, null and undefined, so the fix is to make the left side a real boolean: count > 0 && <p/>, Boolean(count) && <p/>, or a ternary. For defaults, ?? only replaces null and undefined, while || replaces every falsy value. So quantity ?? 1 keeps a real 0, but quantity || 1 would wrongly turn 0 into 1.

What is the difference between `null` and `undefined`?
key_points: `undefined` means a value was never set: an unassigned variable, a missing property, or no return value
`null` is set on purpose to mean "no value"
`typeof undefined` is "undefined", but `typeof null` is "object"

questions.correct_answer: undefined means no value was ever set: you get it from an unassigned variable, a missing property, a missing argument or a function with no return. null is a value that a programmer sets on purpose to say 'empty'. typeof undefined is 'undefined', but typeof null is 'object'. questions.prompt: Why is `typeof null` equal to `"object"`, and how do you check for `null` correctly?
key_points: It is a bug from the first JavaScript engine, where null had the same type tag as objects
It was never fixed because fixing it would break existing websites
Check for null with `value === null`
To check for a real object, use `value !== null && typeof value === "object"`
questions.correct_answer: In the first version of JavaScript, values were stored with a type tag, and null used the same tag as objects, so typeof null returned 'object'. Fixing it would break old websites, so it stayed. To check for null, use value === null. To check for a real object, you need both value !== null and typeof value === 'object'.

questions.prompt: How do you safely read optional data, such as a missing nested field in an API response or an optional prop?
key_points: Optional chaining `?.` stops and returns undefined when a value is null or undefined
Nullish coalescing `??` gives a default only for null or undefined
`== null` checks for both null and undefined at once
Default parameters and destructuring defaults apply only for undefined, not for null
questions.correct_answer: Use optional chaining, like user.profile?.name, which returns undefined instead of throwing when profile is null or undefined. Add a default with ??, which only replaces null and undefined, so a real 0 or empty string is kept. value == null checks for both at once. Be careful that default parameters and destructuring defaults only apply for undefined, so an API that sends null skips your default.
